In our patient with catatonia, in addition to the rigidity, the presence of recent onset of vitiligo, dysautonomia, polyminimyoclonus, oculomotor disturbances, and hyperre flexia suggested the possibility of PERM syndrome, which was confirmed by markedly elevated GAD-65 antibodies in both serum and CSF.

The treatments for both catatonia and SPS also overlap in regards to sharing simil ar symptomatic therapy, such as use of benzodiazepines. 8, 18 Since symptomatic treatment of both catatonia and SPS rely on benzodiazepines, providers may be empiric a l l yt r e a t i n gp a t i e n t sw i t h catatonia caused by SPS without recognizing SPS as the potential etiology. However , the choice of benzodiazepines varies between the cond itions. Diazepam (median dose of 40 mg/day) is known to be effective for SPS while IV lorazepam remains the mainstay of treatment for catatonia. 13 Interestingly, our patient did not respond well to IV benzodiazepines. She only received a 72-hour course prior to stopping this medication for the initiation of E C T . O n ec o u l ds p e c u l a t et h a tt h e l e n g t ho ft i m eo ft r e a t - ment was insufficient, or that the type of benzodiazepine utilized may have an effect on outcome.

Although patients with catatonia may bene fit from benzodiazepines and ECT, additional treatments for SPS and PERM include immunotherapies, such as plasmapheresis, immunoglobulin (IV immunoglobulin), and rituximab. 18, 19 Immunologic therapy resulted in substantial neurologic and cognitive recovery in our patient, and it is thus important to remain vigilant for the above etiologies since diagnosis of such conditions often changes management.

By 4 months after initial presentation, she was ambulating independently and performing all activities of daily living. Her dysphagia improved, and the PEG tube was removed. Eight months after her initial presentation, she has not had any signs of a relapse of her symptoms. Her mood remained stable.

She underwent an intravenous (IV) benzodiazepine challenge of lorazepam 2 mg every 6 hours for 72 hours without improvement of her symptoms. Due to refractory symptoms, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) was initiated on day 4 of her hospitalization, which resulted in mild improvements to her alertness. However, she remained rigid and overall bed-bound. Due to this mild improvement in her alertness, she completed 12 treatments. A PEG tube was placed for dysphagia. The Neurologic Movement Disorders Service was consulted for evaluation of drug-induced parkinsonism given her exposure to a long-acting dopamine antagonist. On neurologic examination, she was encephalopathic, with mild bifacial weakness, oculomotor dysfunction with impaired smooth pursuits, profound axial and limb rigidity, severe dysarthria, and polyminimyoclonus in her jaw, and the distal aspects of her extremities. She was hyperre flexic throughout and she could not ambulate.

During this hospitalization, she received 5 doses of 0. 4 g/kg/day of IV immunoglobulin, 5 days of IV methylprednisolone 1000 mg, and she had noticeable improvement and was able to walk with assistance. Given her severe presentation and slow improvement, 3 days after completing the 5-day course of IV immunoglobulin she underwent 375 mg/m 2 of IV rituximab, followed by second infusion of 375 mg/m 2 15 days after the first dose.
